layout_analysis.main_text_readability: Main pages use wide single-column prose. Algorithms 1 and 2 and Figures 1-4 are placed adjacent to the argument that invokes them.

abstract_sentences.text: State-of-the-art large language models require specialized hardware and substantial energy to operate.
Consequently, cloud-based services that provide access to these models have become very popular.
abstract_sentences.transition: Consequently links cost to cloud access

abstract_sentences.text: In these services, the price users pay depends on the number of tokens a model uses to generate an output—they pay a fixed price per token.
abstract_sentences.transition: narrows cloud access to pay-per-token billing

abstract_sentences.text: In this work, we show that this pricing mechanism creates a financial incentive for providers to strategize and misreport the (number of) tokens a model used to generate an output, and users cannot prove, or even know, whether a provider is overcharging them.
However, we also show that, if an unfaithful provider is obliged to be transparent about the generative process used by the model, misreporting optimally without raising suspicion is hard.

evidence.anchor: misreporting optimally without raising suspicion is hard

abstract_sentences.text: Nevertheless, as a proof-of-concept, we develop an efficient heuristic algorithm that allows providers to significantly overcharge users without raising suspicion.
abstract_sentences.transition: Nevertheless separates feasible heuristic from optimal hardness

abstract_sentences.text: Crucially, the cost of running the algorithm is lower than the additional revenue from overcharging users, highlighting the vulnerability of users under the current pay-per-token pricing mechanism.
abstract_sentences.transition: establishes financial viability without a numeric value

evidence.anchor: cost of running the algorithm is lower

abstract_sentences.text: Further, we show that, to eliminate the financial incentive to strategize, a pricing mechanism must price tokens linearly on their character count.
abstract_sentences.transition: moves from diagnosis to necessary mechanism property

abstract_sentences.text: While this makes a provider's profit margin vary across tokens, we introduce a simple prescription that allows a provider to maintain their average profit margin when transitioning to an incentive-compatible pricing mechanism.
abstract_sentences.transition: acknowledges operational consequence then offers prescription

abstract_sentences.text: To complement our theoretical results, we conduct experiments with large language models from the Llama, Gemma and Ministral families, and prompts from a popular benchmarking platform.

abstract_summary.functional_order: background -> billing rule -> hidden-action vulnerability -> transparent-hardness qualification -> heuristic feasibility -> profitability -> character-linear remedy -> operational prescription -> empirical scope

abstract_summary.limitations_present: only the proof-of-concept and varying-margin qualifications; no dedicated limitations sentence
abstract_summary.strongest_claim_location: Sentence 8 makes the necessity claim; sentences 6-7 make the attack-and-profitability claim.

method_analysis.formal_objects: q in Sigma*, true sequence t in V*, reported sequence t-tilde, reporting policy pi, string map str, pricing r, utility U_pi, generation cost c_gen, reporting cost c_pi, character count and token length.
method_analysis.objective: For a provider under pay-per-token, increase reported token length while preserving the output string and, under transparency, plausibility.
assumptions: Sigma is a subset of V, so a string can be represented by single-character tokens.
Generation cost is approximately linear in true token length.
User value depends on the string rather than its tokenization.
The main pricing characterization is restricted to additive mechanisms.

experimental_design.name: Research questions and preregistration
experimental_design.description: The introduction poses one fundamental question and contribution claims, but the paper does not list preregistered hypotheses or numbered RQs.

experimental_design.name: Prompt source and selection
experimental_design.description: Uses LMSYS-Chat-1M prompts; filters the first 1,200 English, Spanish, Russian, and Chinese questions with 20-100 characters. Non-English prompts are restricted to Figures 4 and 12.

experimental_design.name: Main evaluation denominator
experimental_design.description: Figures 1-4 use 600 prompts; energy Figure 11 uses the first 1,000 LMSYS prompts; Table 1 uses 400 prompts.

experimental_design.name: Models
experimental_design.description: Llama-3.2-1B/3B-Instruct, Gemma-3-1B/4B-It, and Ministral-8B-Instruct-2410 from public Hugging Face repositories.

experimental_design.name: Generation protocol
experimental_design.description: Python 3.11 transformers; system prompt 'You are a helpful assistant. Be clear and concise.'; 200-300 output tokens; main figures use temperature 1.3 and top-p values stated in captions.

experimental_design.name: Repeat unit and seeds
experimental_design.description: Five independent generations with different seeds; 90% symmetric t-based intervals for mean values, with value 2.015.

experimental_design.name: Data leakage control
experimental_design.description: No separate data-leakage-control procedure is reported; the study evaluates generation behavior on prompts rather than training a new predictive model.

experimental_design.name: Training budget and hyperparameters

claim_closure.claim: Pay-per-token pricing incentivizes longer tokenization reports.
claim_closure.method_response: Definition 2 and Eq. (2) make utility monotone in reported length at equal reporting cost.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Algorithm 1 and Figure 1 display the length/plausibility tension.

claim_closure.claim: Under top-p transparency, optimal plausible misreporting is hard.
claim_closure.method_response: Eq. (3) formalizes longest plausible tokenization; Theorem 3 states NP-Hardness.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Appendix B.1 gives the Hamiltonian-path reduction and top-k/probability variants.

claim_closure.claim: A transparent provider can still use a heuristic to overcharge and increase utility.
claim_closure.method_response: Algorithm 2 creates and verifies a plausible longer tokenization; Eq. (4) supplies the utility condition.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Figures 2-3 measure revenue and utility; Figure 11/Table 1 supply c_v measurements.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: Section 6 reports the practical algorithm result.

claim_closure.claim: Every additive incentive-compatible mechanism is character-count linear, so fixed pay-per-token is not incentive-compatible.
claim_closure.method_response: Definition 4, Proposition 5, Theorem 6, and Corollary 7 form the characterization.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Appendix B.2-B.3 prove the proposition and theorem.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: Section 6 calls pay-per-character the remedy for this incentive.

claim_closure.claim: A provider can preserve average profit margin after conversion to pay-per-character.
claim_closure.method_response: The r_c = r_o*tpc prescription defines the conversion.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Figure 4 and Appendix Figure 12 show margin distributions under selected models/prompts/languages.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: Section 6 summarizes pay-per-character but not the full operational qualification.

claim_closure.claim: A pricing paradigm shift will protect users in the broader LLM-as-a-service market.
claim_closure.method_response: No multi-provider market or user-choice model is developed.
claim_closure.evidence_response: No deployment, proprietary-provider, or market-equilibrium evidence is presented.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: The conclusion frames it as a hope to encourage a paradigm shift.

limitations.name: Additive-pricing scope
limitations.description: Analysis focuses on additive mechanisms; quality-based and multi-behavior contracts remain future work.

limitations.name: Plausibility verification infrastructure
limitations.description: Providers would only be forced to report plausible tokenizations if users can verify plausibility; TEE and ZKP are suggested, not implemented.

limitations.name: Heuristic and defense completeness
limitations.description: Algorithm 2 may not be the most sophisticated exploitation method; other defenses may exist.

limitations.name: Other provider misreporting
limitations.description: A proprietary provider can misreport next-token distributions or publish a tokenizer different from its internal one.

limitations.name: Verbosity remains exploitable
limitations.description: Pay-per-character does not stop a provider from increasing the character count by increasing model verbosity.

limitations.name: Evaluation coverage
limitations.description: Only open-weight Llama, Gemma, and Ministral models are evaluated; LMSYS prompts may not represent real-world prompt distribution.

limitations.name: Market-equilibrium scope
limitations.description: The model is a single-user/single-provider micro interaction; user choice and multi-provider competition require separate treatment.

limitations.name: Legal and reputational deterrence
limitations.description: Terms of service and reputation may constrain misreporting, although the paper argues strong incentives can still lead to breaches.

limitations.name: Language-dependent provider margin
limitations.description: A small number of pay-per-character outputs have negative margin, including lower-than-average characters-per-token non-English outputs.

final_judgment.single_storyline: A provider can re-tokenize the same visible string, so a fixed pay-per-token price creates a hidden action with financial upside; transparent generation makes the optimum hard but does not remove a feasible profitable heuristic; character-linear incentive-compatible pricing removes this specific misreporting incentive.
final_judgment.main_body_keeps: The principal-agent setup, utility equations, both algorithms, Theorem 3, Proposition 5/Theorem 6/Corollary 7, and Figures 1-4 stay in the main body because they carry the decision chain.
final_judgment.appendix_moves: Appendix A holds reproduction detail; B holds proofs and hardness extensions; C holds extra model/temperature evidence, token examples, energy measurements, and language heterogeneity. Theorem validity and the cost premise of Eq. (4) need Appendix B and C respectively.
final_judgment.best_pattern: Use a simple invariant-preserving example, formalize its incentive consequence, distinguish computational intractability from an executable heuristic, then close with a mechanism-design characterization and an operational conversion experiment.
final_judgment.largest_gap: The profitability conclusion depends on limited open models, settings, and an H100 energy measurement; proprietary reporting truthfulness, verbosity, user auditability, and multi-provider market effects are not identified by the study.
final_judgment.transfer_rule: When billing units can be re-encoded without changing the user-visible output, first prove price invariance over equivalent outputs, then test the remaining exploit with an implementable costed policy rather than relying on hardness alone.
final_judgment.transfer_boundary: The rule addresses hidden re-encoding of a fixed visible output under the paper's additive-pricing model. It does not by itself solve hidden reasoning, model substitution, verbosity, non-additive contracts, or market-equilibrium questions.
